Habits

Why do I put things off until tomorrow?

Procrastination is not simply laziness: it has a lot to do with how we manage the feelings a task stirs up.

You have a report to write. You know it matters, you know the deadline is close, and yet you end up tidying your desk, answering messages or checking your phone. Voluntarily delaying something we intend to do, even knowing it will cost us, is what psychology calls procrastination.

It is not just a lack of willpower

A widely cited review by Piers Steel (2007) gathered hundreds of studies and found that we procrastinate more when a task feels unpleasant, when the reward is far off and when we are more impulsive or easily distracted. In other words, it depends as much on the task and the moment as on the person.

Other researchers, such as Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl, put it this way: procrastination often works as short-term mood repair. Putting the task off relieves boredom, insecurity or fear of doing it badly for a while. The relief is real, but it is brief, and the pressure comes back stronger.

Your future self, a stranger

Hal Hershfield has shown with brain scans that when we think about ourselves ten years from now, the brain responds in a similar way to when we think about another person. Putting something off until tomorrow is partly handing the problem to a stranger. In his experiments, seeing an aged image of one's own face increased how much people chose to save for retirement. Imagining in detail how you will feel on the day of the deadline can help you get started today.

When it is something more

Very intense and persistent procrastination is common in adult ADHD, in depression, where everything takes more effort, and in perfectionism, where starting means risking doing it badly. In those cases organisational tips help but are not enough: what lies underneath needs attention.

What tends to help

  • Make the task smaller. "Write the report" paralyses; "open the document and write the title and three bullet points" is manageable.
  • Decide when and where. So-called implementation intentions ("if it is 9 o'clock and I am at my desk, I open the report") have shown moderate effects across many studies.
  • Put temptations out of reach: a phone in another room works better than promising not to look at it.
  • Go easier on yourself. In one study of students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam did so less before the next.
When putting everything off comes with persistent sadness, attention difficulties since childhood or paralysing anxiety, it is worth talking to a professional: there may be more going on than a bad habit.

References

  1. Steel, P. (2007). The nature of procrastination. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65–94.
  2. Sirois, F. y Pychyl, T. (2013). Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 7(2), 115–127.
  3. Gollwitzer, P. M. y Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119.
  4. Wohl, M. J. A., Pychyl, T. A. y Bennett, S. H. (2010). I forgive myself, now I can study. Personality and Individual Differences, 48(7), 803–808.
  5. Hershfield, H. E. et al. (2011). Increasing saving behavior through age-progressed renderings of the future self. Journal of Marketing Research, 48(SPL), S23–S37.
